articles.title: Public media freedom has been eroded across central Europe. Now Czechs are rallying to protect theirs
articles.summary: Huge rally planned in Prague to oppose government’s plan to scrap licence fee, which critics say could give ministers more leverage over newsrooms
body: Daniel Stach was an erstwhile junior international slalom kayaker when he first walked into the headquarters of Czech Television in 2010. He had answered a Facebook ad inviting viewers to a behind-the-scenes tour of his favourite programme, a current affairs show called Hyde Park CT24. He did not expect to be offered a job shortly afterwards.

Stach, now 38, presents a science offshoot of that show doing long-form interviews. But he has also emerged as one of the most recognised public faces of the campaign to save the mandatory licence fees that fund the nation’s public broadcasters.

“Czech TV and Czech Radio are the most trusted media organisations in the Czech Republic,” Stach told the Guardian, still wiping the studio makeup off his face in a meeting room at Czech TV. “They are symbols. They are part of our history. They are part of our culture. And that’s why people are standing up for them.”

The first reading of a bill to scrap the licence fees was pushed through in the middle of the night in late October. Since then, thousands of Czechs have taken to the streets in protest at plans to fund the broadcasters from the state budget instead, a move staff fear would give ministers more leverage over their newsrooms.

Organisers say the next rally – planned for this Sunday on Prague’s sprawling Letná Plain – could be the biggest in the country’s post-revolution history. Demonstrators look with nervousness to countries across central and eastern Europe – most notably neighbouring Slovakia but also Hungary, Poland and Serbia, where under previous rightwing populist governments media independence was severely weakened.

The prime minister, Andrej Babiš, has said his coalition of populist, hard-right nationalist and Eurosceptic parties will not be deterred by the protests, although he has suggested a number of alternative models including voluntary payments.

Staff at both broadcasters went on strike on 3 November, and demonstrations were held in 21 towns and cities across the country. During the strike Stach and fellow reporters, dressed in black, read on-air announcements from pieces of paper.

Some of the programming on 3 November was replaced with archive material. In place of its usual morning news programme, Czech TV’s rolling news channel showed old footage of the communist-era president Gustáv Husák touring the Prague metro.

It was a subtle nod to what campaigners say is in store for viewers if the changes go ahead, although one government minister said he thought the archive reports were an improvement on the station’s regular programming.
Stach conceded some of those attending the nationwide protests were channelling wider opposition to Babiš’s government, which came to power a year ago.
Babiš has accused the opposition and some journalists of firing up the public with unfounded claims the editorial independence of the two organisations is at risk.
He even compared a night-time protest outside parliament – the first reading of the bill to scrap the fees was scheduled for 4.36am – to the 6 January assault on the Capitol in Washington.
Police in Prague said one person was detained after throwing a cobblestone in the direction of the lower house. There were no reported arrests or injuries.

The culture ministry, which drew up the draft legislation, did not respond to a request for an interview. But last week Babiš published an op-ed on what he called the “seven lies” being peddled by the opposition over the licence fees, which together add up to 205 koruna (£7.03) per month.

“Anyone who talks about ‘nationalisation’ [of public media] is deliberately lying,” he wrote, describing the criticism as “hysterical outbursts”. “Under no circumstances will we interfere in editorial work.”
The prime minister, 72, argued that guaranteeing the broadcasters’ funding by law – and automatically adjusting it for inflation – would reduce politicians’ direct influence.
Babiš, who acknowledged that the funding model could still change during the bill’s second reading, has ruled out raising taxes to pay for the change.

The Czech leader has repeatedly said that public media in 17 of the EU’s 27 countries is funded directly by the state. Government figures often point to “the Nordic model” as an example of where scrapping the licence fee can work.

There is in fact no single Nordic model. Finland and Sweden replaced their licence fees with compulsory levies earmarked for public broadcasting. Denmark funds its national broadcasters from general taxation. Non-EU member Norway does the same.
The Czech proposal would cut funding to both broadcasters by about 15%, reversing an increase introduced by the previous centre-right government in 2025.
The Babiš government says funding will return to 2024 levels, at a time when all public institutions are being asked to save money.

The broadcasters say this is disingenuous, as the licence fee had been frozen since 2008 with no allowance for inflation. “We’re talking about funding as if it was an issue of its own, but we also know there is a backlash against public service media that is being weaponised by some of the political forces in Czechia,” said Thibaut Bruttin, the director general of the global press freedom organisation Reporters Without Borders.

“So we can’t pretend that this assault on the funding is not also a way to undermine the quality, the capacity, and the trust in public service media,” Bruttin said during a visit to the Czech capital.
Bruttin, like other critics of the Czech proposals, says they risk repeating what happened in neighbouring Slovakia.

There, public broadcasting has been brought under tighter state control by the ultranationalist culture minister, Martina Šimkovičová, a former TV presenter who rose to prominence promoting conspiracy theories on YouTube.

Observers also question the timing of the bill. The first reading was fast-tracked through parliament weeks after bruising senate and local election defeats for Babiš’s ANO party and his far-right, Eurosceptic coalition partners.

articles.title: Yalta became a byword for betrayal. Will Trump, Xi and Putin enact another carve-up?
articles.summary: Russia and US approach potential summit seeking China’s help to extricate them from wars of choice, as Putin hopes to find consensus on new global order
body: The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, is among those who have expressed concern that the world will witness a Yalta 2.0 moment if Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin meet trilaterally, as expected, on the sidelines of the Apec summit in China next week.

It is a truism in diplomacy that if you are not around the table, the risk is that you, or your values, are on the menu and about to be carved up. Many excluded from the summit in Shenzhen, principally Ukraine but also eastern Europe and Baltic countries, Taiwan and even Iran, have reason to be nervous that their sponsors might abandon them in a complex geopolitical trade-off that Putin envisions, and Trump seems to endorse.

Putin has long proposed this re-enactment of the greatest wartime summit, held in February 1945 at Joseph Stalin’s insistence in a rundown Tsarist resort on the south coast of Crimea alongside Franklin D Roosevelt and Winston Churchill.
Trump has cast himself in the role of the enthusiastic guest while Xi acts the bashful host, ever reluctant to embrace the status of a traditional global superpower.

No one quite knows what will happen if the three men meet or even if China will allow more than a stiff protocol-driven exchange of statements. China is already trying to push nuclear disarmament off the agenda.

It may prove to be little more than abbreviated geopolitical theatre that Putin can retail domestically to show that Russia – even with an economy seven times smaller than that of the EU – still plays with the big boys.

But if Putin has his way he will try to ensure that this becomes the first of a series of meetings in this format in which the big powers organise a new world order on a set of security oriented principles in which liberal values play little part.

As Russia’s chief negotiator, Vladimir Medinsky, told Russian TV: “The task is to create a comprehensive system of comprehensive security in Europe that will become a new modern Yalta or Potsdam. If we manage to create such a security system then we will ensure peace in Europe for decades, perhaps even centuries. That is our main task.”

Russia’s foreign ministry spokesperson, Maria Zakharova, said the summit could mark “the start of a return from this slide into absolute chaos to stabilisation”. For Zelenskyy, the concern is that almost any time Putin and Trump converse, it is Kyiv that suffers.

The original Yalta is widely remembered, outside Russia, as a moment of cynical trade-offs, even ignominy, to rival the appeasement of the 1938 Munich agreement. It was eight days that shaped the postwar world in which absent countries were discarded or divided by the imminent wartime victors.

FDR, months from death, was intent on enlisting Russian support for a new League of Nations organisation and for Russian participation in the war against Japan. In return, he accepted the fait accompli of Russia’s presence in Poland, and covered his treacherous tracks by persuading Stalin to sign a declaration that affirmed the principles of “sovereign rights and self-government” should prevail in countries freed from Nazi rule.

Few thought the dictator had any intent to honour the agreement. Indeed, honour was somewhat absent throughout the eight days. When Churchill told Stalin it was a “matter of honour” that the independence of Poland, Britain’s original casus belli, was preserved, Stalin replied the issue for him was “a matter of life and death”. Churchill had no means to confront Stalin since by then he was the victor of Stalingrad and Kursk, and the commander of an army that had crushed Germany.

The subsequent sense of shame about the betrayal of Yalta accumulated mostly in America, so much so that in May 2005, before a trip to Moscow for the 60th anniversary of Victory in Europe Day, George Bush told an audience in Latvia that Yalta had “consigned millions to communist captivity. When powerful nations negotiated, the freedom of small nations was somehow expendable. Yet this attempt to sacrifice freedom for the sake of stability left a continent divided and unstable.” It was a view shared across Europe.

The Republican tradition expressed by Bush has been expunged by Trump. In his 2025 national security document, Trump lauded the sphere of influence geopolitics championed at Yalta. He named the western hemisphere as America’s domain. It remained deferential to Russia and China’s spheres.

Unfortunately, Trump took little notice of the strategy prepared for him. He retained his respect for Putin and Xi, but indulged himself, and Israel, in a disastrous imperial overreach elsewhere, notably in Iran.

As a result, the US and Russia are approaching the summit seeking China’s help to extricate them from wars of choice that have wounded them. Xi is cast in the role of Stalin, hosting two countries in need of his beneficence.

It leaves China somewhat wary, reluctant to use its leverage if it helps the US, or is seen to run counter to the Chinese narrative of being a force for stability and coexistence. Speaking at the Emirates Policy Center conference in Abu Dhabi, Prof Minghao Zhao from Fudan University gave a classic exposition of Chinese non-interference. “The Russia-Ukraine war is the strategic mistake made by the Russian president. The Iran war is the strategic mistake made by President Trump. China is managing the consequences of those conflicts.”

By contrast, Dr Wang Huiyao, the president of the Center for China and Globalization and an early advocate of a trilateral summit, argued China was needed. He referenced the Kindleberger trap – a period of chaos caused by too little global leadership. He said China was trying to be helpful by propping up multilateralism and might provide guarantees in Iran, something the Iranian leadership favours, but even he saw China’s stabilisation role largely through the prism of developing the global economy.
In short, China might help extricate Trump in the Middle East. After all, open waterways are necessary to meet its insatiable demand for oil.

But China sees Ukraine as a strictly European security issue in which it is not willing to betray Putin, or endorse a settlement reached without Europe’s agreement. China is in the midst of repairing relations with Europe after China’s industrial overcapacity in 2025 flooded the European market, risking its deindustrialisation. China’s embrace of Putin’s vision of a new European security architecture would infuriate Germany and the European Commission.

For some, such as John Ikenberry, the theorist of liberal internationalism, the sight of the US president carving up the world with autocrats is anathema. He thinks there is a viable alliance of democracies.

But Charles Kupchan, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, says more Yaltas are the future. “We have to learn to work across the geopolitical and ideological dividing lines,” he said. “We are now in a world in which the US and its democratic allies are no longer the preponderant coalition.
“Who is coming up? China, India, Indonesia, large countries of the global south – all of then playing the field and most of them have closer economic ties with China than with the US.

“We are going to have to learn to work with autocracies and to live with them more comfortably. Is there a downside risk? Sure. Might Trump throw Taiwan and Ukraine under the bus? Possibly, but I doubt it. But we need to break the ice. These conversations have to start now and I give credit to President Trump for starting it.”

articles.title: Terror from the skies: drones are redefining warfare in Sudan, and massacring its civilians
articles.summary: Strikes with huge death tolls are an increasing occurrence as UAVs ‘bring the war to places that were once safe’
body: The first drone struck the busy transport hub near a market in Al-Dibab as hundreds of people gathered to board trucks to take them back to their homes.
Ten minutes later on the evening of 18 October, a second drone hit the same site in the town in West Kordofan state, Sudan. At least 139 people were killed.

Eight days after the “double-tap” attack – designed to maximise casualties by killing and injuring emergency responders, volunteers and bystanders on top of the original victims – a drone hit a busy market in Nyala, the capital of South Darfur.

Emergency Lawyers, a rights group tracking violence in Sudan, put the death toll from that attack at 103. “I lost my 19-year-old son,” a Nyala resident told Agence France-Presse. “We buried him alongside more than 70 bodies in a single site.”

These are just two of a relentless series of mass casualty drone strikes in recent months in Sudan, where the use of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) has risen sharply, becoming the leading cause of civilian deaths by far in the country’s civil war. Drones killed at least 306 people and injured hundreds more in the first three weeks of October alone, according to the UN.

Sudan’s civil war broke out when a power struggle between the armed forces and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces erupted into violence in the capital, Khartoum, in April 2023. A humanitarian catastrophe has unfolded in the intervening years. Estimates of the death toll so far vary from 150,000 to more than 400,000. Millions more have been driven from their homes. Vast swathes of the population face acute food insecurity.

The dynamics of the warfare have evolved over the past 42 months. At the start, the army relied on fighter jets, attack helicopters, tanks and long-range artillery. The RSF heavily depended on pick-ups mounted with machine guns and anti-aircraft guns, in addition to anti-tank weapons and rocket launchers.

A Sudan investigator at the Centre for Information Resilience, which conducts open-source investigations, said the organisation first documented the use of weaponised drones in the conflict in July 2023, and that the frequency has increased significantly over time. “Now you hear about a drone strike nearly every day,” he said.
A CIR investigation published last month identified 21 unique UAV models – both surveillance-reconnaissance drones and combat drones – that had been used in Sudan since the start of the war.
It found 10 models used by RSF and aligned forces, manufactured in Belarus, China, and Russia; and five models used by the Sudanese army and aligned forces, manufactured in Iran, Sudan, and Turkey.

A Sudan investigator at CIR said FPV drones – often smaller quadcopters used as kamikaze drones – were common earlier in the war, but that the warring parties were increasingly turning to larger UAVs with very long ranges that could carry precision-guided munitions.

Ali Mahmoud Ali, a Sudan analyst at the conflict monitoring group Acled, said the Sudanese armed forces usually used drones to hit RSF bases and cut fuel and other supply routes to areas controlled by the group, while the militia often targeted infrastructure, such as power stations, water stations, airports, and hospitals “to send the message” that it could “destabilise SAF [army] regions”.
He added that drones helped secure troops on the ground for whoever had the upper hand in the air, making ground operations easier. “The key weapon in peripheral warfare is the drone,” Ali said.

Between January and April of this year, drone strikes accounted for at least 880 civilian deaths – more than 80% of all conflict-related civilian deaths in that timeframe – according to the UN Human Rights Office.
CIR data shows the most-struck targets are commercial spaces such as markets, residential areas, and military assets and sites.

Ali Salih*, a resident of El Obeid, the capital of North Kordofan, has grown accustomed to drone attacks in the area and, like other residents, lives with the constant fear of when the next one may strike.

He recalled being at home when the most recent drone attack hit the city, a strike he said killed three people and injured several others. “Although we try to continue our daily lives, the repeated attacks make things difficult, especially for people living near areas that may be targeted,” he said.

In early November, Denise Brown, the UN resident and humanitarian coordinator in Sudan, said the intensifying drone attacks were disrupting electricity, water and fuel supplies, as well as hampering the delivery of humanitarian aid.

“We need help passing the message to whoever needs to hear it, that this must stop,” she said. “People who need life-saving dialysis can’t get it. Women are giving birth with no lights in the hospital. Operations can’t take place.”

James Elder, a spokesperson for Unicef, said on Tuesday two-thirds of child injuries and deaths in Sudan this year were caused by drones. “They are bringing the war to places that were once safe,” he said. “People here talk about three things: safety, education and water. Armed drones are taking all three.”

Drone warfare is also affecting regional dynamics. On 19 October, a drone strike allegedly targeting an RSF fuel depot in Abyei, a border region disputed by Sudan and South Sudan, killed at least 153 people when it hit a market in the area.

Sudan’s foreign ministry said late last month that a wave of drones used in attacks by the RSF on electricity infrastructure in army-held areas were supplied by the United Arab Emirates and launched from Ethiopia. Both the UAE and Ethiopia deny supporting the RSF.

Not only have drones reshaped the civil war, they have also “muddied the water of attribution”, a Sudan investigator at CIR said. Christy Cooney, a researcher at the NGO Avaaz, said drones enabled the combatants to attack each other across vast distances from far behind the frontlines and offer a degree of unpredictability over ground attacks. “There’s obviously no warning,” he said.

Nathaniel Raymond, the executive director of the Humanitarian Research Lab at the Yale School of Public Health, said the mass killing carried out by the RSF in the town of El Fasher last year, which the UN has said had “hallmarks of genocide”, was made technically possible by the presence of drones and “the tactical integration of UAV systems into a repertoire of civilian hunter-killer targeting”.
He said the tactics and strategies being implemented by the army and RSF could become the future of war around the world if there was no international control on how wars involving UAVs were fought.

“What we are seeing here is the coming attraction of the future – unbridled civilian target-focused application of now increasingly cheaper, effective point-and-click warfare,” Raymond said. “What is happening in Sudan this year with drones will redefine the next decade-plus of war more than the tank and the biplane did in the first world war.”
* Name changed for safety reasons

articles.title: University hounded out of Hungary by Orbán reaches out to new government
articles.summary: Prospect of partial return to Budapest by Central European University suggests confidence in Hungary’s future
body: A university that Viktor Orbán tried to chase out of Hungary is open to expanding its presence in Budapest, in a mark of confidence in the country’s democratic future.

Carsten Q Schneider, the interim president and rector of Central European University (CEU), said it was interested in increasing its programmes in Budapest, as long as this did not damage the student experience.

So far the CEU has not held formal talks with Hungary’s new government, which has promised to restore academic freedom, “but our hand is reaching out, their hand is reaching out – it is just that they have many things to do”, the academic told the Guardian.

The CEU relocated its main activities to Vienna from Budapest in 2019, after pressure from the previous government led by Orbán. But the outlook changed when Péter Magyar won a landslide victory in April pledging to root out corruption and reform the state.

The CEU, founded by Hungarian-American financier and philanthropist George Soros in 1991 to entrench democratic change in the region, was forced to cease awarding degrees in Budapest in response to a law widely seen as targeting the institution.

The EU’s highest court struck down Hungary’s “Lex CEU” in 2020, finding that it violated the EU charter of fundamental rights, but the verdict came too late for the university. The CEU retains 312 staff in Budapest, mostly administrative, but the majority, 476, and all its teaching, are in Vienna.

Schneider said upgrading the status of the CEU, which is privately funded, in Budapest would be “a symbol for academic freedom [and] of resilience” but depended on goodwill and funding independent of the Hungarian government. He said a decision on its future in Hungary would be taken by the CEU’s 13-member board, whose members include Soros and his son, Alexander Soros.
“We don’t want special treatment,” Schneider said. ‘“We are a great asset, so let’s work out something.”

But the CEU, which he said was “thriving tremendously” in Vienna, does not plan a wholesale return to Budapest. Any change would have to ensure the quality of the student experience, for instance, assuring that students would be able to combine courses, say in economics and history, without having to travel the 200km-plus distance between the two cities.
Focused on social sciences, law and humanities, the CEU has more than 1,400 students from 103 countries, mostly doing master’s and PhD programmes.

According to Schneider, for the first time in the CEU’s 25-year history, students from the US now make up the largest cohort of master’s students (10%). The CEU has seen an increase in US applicants since Donald Trump returned to the White House and launched a sweeping campaign against elite universities, including slashing federal funding and seeking to exert control over internal policies.

The CEU rector has had informal talks with US academics on how to maintain academic freedom under pressure from rightwing populists. He described his message as: “Don’t be naive for a second. These people have a plan, so it’s not by accident that they attack universities. They want to have cultural hegemony.” He added, however, that Trump and allied movements, such as Germany’s Alternative für Deutschland, have identified “real problems”, such as in the US how universities have entrenched “a reproduction of elites”

When coming under political pressure, he said universities needed “to look for allies”, among other academic institutions, students, alumni and parents. Institutions also had to stand up for disciplines under attack, such as gender studies, Schneider added.
He recalled the outpouring of support for CEU – when tens of thousands of people protested in Budapest in defence of the university – as “one of the most humbling experiences I have had”.
Schneider, a German political scientist who specialises in the study of democracies and regime transition, said Magyar had successfully used Orbán’s political machine against him.
Related: Viktor Orbán’s brother detained in people-smuggling investigation, Hungarian PM says

“Nobody has a better idea than [Magyar] how to defeat the most potent and the most skilled illiberal populist [Orbán]. So he knows something.” He added: “The people and skills that you need to bring a non-democratic regime down are not the same and sometimes the opposite of what it takes to establish a democracy. So the question now is whether he [Magyar] has the skills to basically reinvent liberal democracy for the 21st century.”

Schneider said Hungary could be the world’s first “post-illiberal democracy” – a model for democratic restoration, just as Orbán inspired rightwing populists around the world. But he also raised doubts about this thesis, saying there were questions about how Magyar and his Tisza party might develop in the context of Hungary’s “very difficult economic situation”.

The test would be, he suggested, when Magyar faces losing support and, eventually, defeat at the ballot box. “So what happens when he loses support and then cracks in his movement appear? Will he be the visionary leader who manages … to establish a three, four, five-party system, where people compete? That is to be seen.”

articles.title: US-bound flights out of Australia delayed after telecommunications outage grounded American planes
articles.summary: Sydney and Melbourne airports say flights were affected by now-lifted ban on departures in US
body: Some US-bound flights from Sydney airport were grounded or delayed on Saturday after American authorities halted departures and delayed landings at all US airports.
Flights from Melbourne airport were also affected, with travel for passengers expected to depart for Los Angeles shortly after 10am being delayed by almost three hours.
Sydney airport confirmed the US ban on flight arrivals was lifted shortly before 1pm, although it was not known how this would impact delays.
Earlier, the airport confirmed some US-bound flights had been grounded.
“We are aware of the nationwide ground stop issued by the US Federal Aviation Administration and are monitoring the situation closely,” the spokesperson said.
“Passengers travelling to or via the United States should check with their airline for the latest information regarding their flight.”

Passengers on US bound flights from Sydney Airport reported being stuck on the tarmac for three hours before eventually departing. One plane required extra fuel after running air-conditioning for several hours while waiting.
The FAA announced the nationwide pause in response to “a temporary telecommunications outage”. It has since lifted the grounding order, as it continued to investigate the cause of the outage.
Passengers on two US-bound flights from Melbourne airport, which were due to depart at 12pm and 12.45pm, were also delayed due to the situation in the US.
A flight to Dallas, scheduled for 10am, departed at around 1pm, shortly after the US ban was lifted.
By 3pm Saturday, all delayed flights from Melbourne had departed.
Qantas thanked passengers for their patience and recommended people with upcoming flights to the US to check its website for more information.
Four flights from Brisbane were also delayed.. Two had departed by 3pm on Saturday.
“Passengers travelling to North America are advised to contact their airline for the latest information about their flight,” a Brisbane Airport spokesperson said.

articles.title: Flights slowly resume after US aviation agency lifts nationwide ground stop
articles.summary: Transportation secretary Sean Duffy says the airspace is now open and the problem has been identified
body: Flights in the US have slowly started resuming after being grounded for several hours on Friday due to a major communications outage, but authorities have warned that a return to normal operations will take time.

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) lifted a nationwide ground stop about four hours after it was declared on Friday afternoon, delaying or canceling more than 11,000 US flights, according to aviation tracker FlightAware, and throwing airports into sudden chaos.

The FAA confirmed the airspace was open in an advisory on its website. “So at 8.15 tonight, Eastern Time, we’ve opened up the airspace,” Sean Duffy, the US transportation secretary, said. “But it’s going to take us some time to unwind what’s happened this afternoon.”
Duffy said the federal government had “identified the problem” that brought down the US air traffic control system on Friday and the system “is operational right now”.
At a White House briefing on Friday evening, Duffy said the trouble began at 3.36pm, when air traffic control centres experienced ​instability in radar and communications systems.

“What we have is an incredibly old air traffic control system,” he said. “Our routers actually got overloaded with data, and … they started to give us inconsistency in the data from those routers. And because of that, we shut the system down.”

But the briefing on Friday evening with Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, quickly turned into a plea for funding from Congress to “fully fund a full build of a brand new air traffic control system”.
A notice from the FAA had earlier said the ground stop was imposed “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety”.
Duffy said more than 3,500 airplanes were in the air when the ground stop was issued.
Mullin said in a news conference that preliminary investigations into the stoppage did not indicate that it was tied to a “nefarious attack”.
“There’s no indication as of yet that this was a nefarious attack against it. It’s just a telecommunications outage as of right now,” he told reporters.

The flight grounding caused widespread chaos and left hundreds of thousands of passengers in limbo. Footage from airports around the country showed gates full, with planes waiting on taxiways. Passengers thronged concourses, desperate for information about an outage that had thrown their plans into chaos.

As news of the airspace reopening trickled down to airline passengers on Friday evening, not all greeted the news with joy. A woman at John F Kennedy airport in New York who gave her name as simply Lola said she was frustrated. She had already rebooked her flight to Atlanta for another day and was going home. “I don’t like it,” she said.
Amid the earlier confusion at US airports, the California governor, Gavin Newsom, called the Trump administration to offer more clarity to passengers who are trying to get to their destinations.

“Americans are stuck at airports across the country. They deserve answers, clear updates, and a plan to get home safely. Instead, the Trump Administration is correcting reporters on AI’s “preferred name”. These are not serious people,” Newsom wrote in a post on X, in reference to Mullin correcting a reporter’s use of the term AI earlier in the day.

In an interview on CNN, US congressman Ro Khanna said that he is waiting to be briefed on what exactly led to the technical issues and sparked the ground stoppage and for more public-facing communications from the transportation secretary.

“There’s a lot of nervousness,” Khanna said of the feeling among passengers. “We’re waiting to be briefed in Congress about what, exactly, has happened. We just need communication from them. If they were there every hour briefing the American public, it would help and give us a sense of a timeline.”

According to CNN, the FAA told airlines that the outages are the result of router malfunctions that are believed to have originated at Chicago Midway international airport and rippled across the rest of the US.
The FAA said in a statement that they “thoroughly tested” their systems to confirm they were stable and reliable before clearing flights to resume.
San Francisco international airport announced in a social media post that flights bound for Hawaii and Asia were cleared to depart.
John F Kennedy airport posted on its social media that travelers should confirm flight status with the airline before heading to the airport.
US airlines including United, Delta, Southwest and American Airlines announced they were resuming flights on Friday night after the ground stop was lifted.
United said it was restarting operations, “including some Friday night flights”, while American Airlines said it was focused on “operating as many remaining flights as possible this evening”.

British Airways cancelled a flight to New York that had been due to take off from Heathrow at 10.30pm on Friday night, and a spokesperson for Manchester airport confirmed three US-bound flights scheduled to leave on Saturday morning – all operated by Virgin Atlantic – were likely to be affected if the issue was not resolved soon.
A ground-stop order by the FAA requires that aircraft remain on the ground and bars them from taking off. Planes already in the air are usually allowed to remain in the air.

This is the third time all departing flights have been grounded in the US. The first time was on 11 September 2011; the other was in January 2023, when the FAA paused all ⁠domestic departures for less than two hours after a pilot notification system malfunctioned.
The FAA has more than 14,000 air traffic controllers who handle the more than 44,000 flights that take off from airports across the US each day, according to FAA data.

Last week, the FAA announced that the first digital air traffic control towers in the US were officially operational in Alaska and Florida, as part of a modernization project intended to reduce flight delays and improve the flow of air traffic.
Last year, ​Congress ​approved $12.5bn to fix ​the FAA’s ageing communications system, and ​on Friday ‌the FAA ​and ​White House asked Congress for another $30.1bn to address other issues.

articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: Zelenskyy says Starshield restrictions continue on ‘entire front line’
articles.summary: Curbs on SpaceX system are making it hard to intercept drones and sending bad signal to Russia, says Ukrainian president. What we know on day 1,725
body: Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said ⁠speed restrictions remain in place on the US Starshield satellite communications system, hampering ⁠the Ukrainian military’s ability ⁠to ​operate inside the country. The continued restrictions made it hard to intercept jet-powered and other ⁠drones and sent a bad signal to Russia on dealing with land seized by Russian forces ⁠in the war, the Ukrainian president also said on Friday. “Unfortunately, the speed restrictions remain in place ​along the entire front line ‌and in temporarily-occupied ‌territories of Ukraine,” he said in his nightly video address. “I expect ‌the ministry of defence and the foreign ministry, together with all relevant structures in the United States, will work through this issue.” Ukrainian officials said in mid-October that Elon Musk’s SpaceX had abruptly capped the speed of Starlink and its Starshield military version amid tensions with ​the US over Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries. Service was restored on 24 October.

Zelenskyy said on Thursday Ukrainian military units had recorded ​disruptions to ​Starshield over several days. He repeated that the restrictions “limit our ​ability to ‌intercept jet-powered ​Shaheds [Iranian-designed drones] ​and counter other drones”. “They also send Russia a signal that America may somehow treat our temporarily-occupied land differently,” he said. “We expect the speed to be restored.”

Russia attacked a hospital in the centre of Kyiv, close to several western embassies, after Zelenskyy’s comments on the throttling of Starshield . Three people were injured when a drone smashed into the National Institute of Traumatology and Orthopedics at 3am, hitting the second floor of the hospital and an adjoining 19th-century building in the capital, reports Luke Harding. Meanwhile, Russia claimed to have shot down nearly 1,200 Ukrainian drones overnight, one of the largest swarms sent by Kyiv. It said at least four people were killed in the southern region of Volgograd.

The EU’s foreign policy chief warned against “walking into the traps that Russia is setting” as she said Moscow was trying to start a debate about European security in order to divert attention from its aggression, reports Jennifer Rankin. “We have one aggressor and one victim, and the aggressor does not have security concerns,” Kaja Kallas said on arrival at an EU leaders’ summit in Dublin. In talks on the Ukraine war, Russia has revived its hardline demands for a total overhaul of European security – demands that were rejected in 2021.

Russia has been rocked by two car bomb attacks that killed a senior military figure and seriously injured a suspected intelligence agent, in the latest in a series of assassination attempts believed to have been orchestrated by Kyiv. On Friday morning a car bomb exploded in southern Moscow, severely injuring Sergei Zavorotniy, 72, a former senior aide to Ukraine’s exiled former prime minister Mykola Azarov, reports Pjotr Sauer. The blast came a day after a car bomb explosion in St Petersburg killed a senior Russian military official. The official has not been publicly identified but a local broadcaster cited sources as saying the victim was a colonel in the Russian air force.

Russian forces launched strikes on two ⁠Ukrainian cities on Friday, killing one person ⁠and injuring more than ⁠50 ​in the south-eastern city of Zaporizhzhia and killing ⁠two more in the Black Sea port of ⁠Odesa, regional officials said. In Zaporizhzhia, a ​five-storey apartment ‌building was ‌hit and seriously damaged. A rescue worker was killed when a concrete slab collapsed during operations to clear rubble, regional governor ‌Mykhailo Semikin said. In Odesa, two people died in an ⁠attack on a private residence, ​said the city’s military administration hed, Serhiy Lysak. Five people ​were ​injured.

A general in Ukraine’s SBU security service suspected in a serious corruption case was released from pre-trial detention on Friday after posting $1.2m bail. Footage on Ukraine’s TSN.ua news site showed Serhiy Duka after leaving prison proclaiming his innocence and thanking his SBU “brothers-in-arms” who had raised the bail money. Duka was detained on 4 November as part of an anti-corruption operation targeting an alleged criminal group that investigators say involved members of the SBU, the prosecutor’s office, the police and organised crime.

articles.title: What to know about the rare nationwide ground stop issued by the FAA
articles.summary: The Federal Aviation Administration issued a ground stop for all planes due to take off in the US, delaying and canceling thousands of flights
body: The US Federal ⁠Aviation Administration said in a statement that the nationwide halt to departures and delays to landings at all US airports that began at about 4pm ET on Friday was caused by “a temporary telecommunications outage”.
“Every flight has been accounted for and international flights will be handled on a case by case basis,” the FAA added.
Here is what we know about the rare nationwide ground stop issued by the FAA.
Related: Nationwide FAA ground stop: nearly 11,000 flights delayed or canceled at airports across the US

The FAA lifted the ground stop at 8.15pm ET Friday. In a White House briefing, Markwayne Mullin, homeland security secretary, and Sean Duffy, the US transportation secretary, appeared to suggest that the cause of Friday’s outage was that older technology became overwhelmed with data after new technology was introduced. The FAA announced three days ago that a new air traffic management tool, known as Smart, was activated at all 22 air route traffic control centers in the US.

“What it appears to be right now is”, Mullin said, “as secretary Duffy and FAA was going in and putting patches into the system, they were putting new equipment and new technology and that new equipment, new technology just wasn’t- it was overwhelming the older system, which is why secretary Duffy made it very clear the patchwork doesn’t work. We need one complete system. We need someone to come in and build the whole system. Doing it nickel- and dime-ing it together does not work. This is what happens when that takes place.”
Duffy denied the new Smart system, which incorporates artificial intelligence, had caused the problem.
Mullin said at the briefing: “We’ve seen zero evidence that this was a cyber-attack.”

“Now, when we start looking at cyber threats, cyber-attacks, typically some people are going to raise their hand up and say, ‘hey, we did that.’ There’s no chatter. We haven’t seen any footprints, as you would say, or identifications of people that got into the system,” Mullin added. “It appears that this was mechanically driven.”

There have been 10,543 flight delays within, into, or out of the US so far, according to the website FlightAware, and 3,580 cancellations. Duffy said that more than 3,500 airplanes were in the air when the ground stop was issued.

A ground-stop order by the FAA requires that aircraft remain on the ground and bars them from taking off. Planes already in the air are usually allowed to remain in the air. The FAA has more than 14,000 air traffic controllers who handle the more than 44,000 flights that take off from airports across the US each day, according to FAA data.

Duffy and Mullin used Friday night’s briefing as a chance to plead for funding from Congress. “The president for the last year has been asking Congress to fully fund a full build of a brand new air traffic control system,” Duffy said. “I want Congress to give us emergency funding,” Duffy said later. “I want $50bn. President Trump is a builder. He is going to build this network, and deliver for the American people.”
Both men peppered their remarks with lavish praise for Donald Trump, who was curiously quiet during the crisis that lasted for more than four hours.
Last year, ​Congress ​approved $12.5bn to fix ​the FAA’s ageing communications system, and ​on Friday ‌the FAA ​and ​White House asked Congress for another $30.1bn to address other issues.
This is just the second nationwide ​ground stop of all departures since the 9/11 attacks. The previous one came in January 2023, when the FAA paused all ⁠domestic departures for less than two hours.

articles.title: Russia is ‘setting traps’ in Ukraine talks, EU foreign policy chief warns
articles.summary: Kaja Kallas says Moscow is trying to divert attention from its aggression by raising issue of European security
body: The EU’s foreign policy chief has warned against “walking into the traps that Russia is setting” as she said Moscow was trying to start a debate about European security in order to divert attention from its aggression.

“We have one aggressor and one victim, and the aggressor does not have security concerns,” Kaja Kallas said on arrival at an EU leaders’ summit in Dublin. “Nobody has ever attacked them. They have attacked others. I mean, keep the focus, people.”

In talks on the Ukraine war, Russia has revived its hardline demands for a total overhaul of European security – demands that were rejected in 2021 because they were seen as an infringement of the sovereignty of central and eastern European countries. The latest round of talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US was held this week in Abu Dhabi.

Donald Trump’s envoy and son-in-law, Jared Kushner, said on Thursday night that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to expand the next round of peace negotiations to include the Europeans. However, Russia quickly contradicted that assurance.

European leaders have long said they will support Ukraine in any peace talks, but want to see a ceasefire before negotiations. They also stress the continent has an extensive web of security agreements that Russia has violated.

Friedrich Merz, the German chancellor, said: “Russia wants to talk about questions of a European security architecture. We do not need to discuss that; it already exists.” He added that it was a “given” that his country would be part of any European delegation.
The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said it was “self-explanatory that Europe is included in the peace talks to safeguard our interests, but also to support Ukraine”.

The Kremlin said on Friday: “Once we understand [Europe’s] real intentions and their willingness to contribute to the peace process, then we can make a decision on holding talks in an expanded format.” Russia’s lead negotiator in Abu Dhabi, Vladimir Medinsky, said it was “unclear what there is to discuss” with Europe.
The US call to involve Europe in talks has turned the spotlight on who would represent it.

Speaking after a summit of EU leaders in Dublin on Friday, the European Council president, António Costa, said leaders had agreed on a negotiating team: the EU institutions and E5 countries, namely Britain, France, Germany, Italy and Poland.
“Europe must speak with one clear and united voice in all discussions that shape the future of Ukraine and the security of our continent,” he said. “This is ultimately a team effort.”

The format had already emerged in recent months, but the need to formalise the grouping gained momentum after Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, this week urged his European allies to decide who will represent Europe in negotiations.

Kushner also mocked the absence of a single person to speak for the entire continent. “If Europe could identify one person to speak on their behalf, that would be a bigger achievement than getting the Russians to include them in the negotiations,” he said earlier this week.

But there was an increasingly settled view that Europe would not be represented by a single person, but by different interlocutors from the wider continent. Paris and Berlin had argued for a continued role for their own envoys in the E3 format of Britain, France and Germany, alongside EU representatives. Smaller member states put the emphasis more firmly on the EU representatives: Costa and Kallas, the EU’s high representative for foreign affairs and security policy.
Earlier in the day, Sweden’s prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, said the discussion on who should represent Europe was “slightly overstated” as it had differing interests.

Some of the issues in peace talks were “pure EU interests”, he said, citing financing Kyiv and Ukraine’s future membership in the bloc. He also supported other formats, such as the “pretty uncomplicated” E3 and the “very legitimate” E5, which includes Italy and Poland, as well as a role for EU representatives. He said: “I am quite flexible on that. I think what we actually say is more important than the exact configuration of the people in the room.”

Several at the summit, including Kallas, also pointed to the importance of including the UK, a founder member of the coalition of the willing, a broad group of countries committed to future peacekeeping in Ukraine.
Ireland’s taoiseach, Micheál Martin, said the UK and Norway each had a significant role and “that all has to be taken into consideration because it’s a European, continent-wide issue”.

The British prime minister, Andy Burnham, said it was for the EU to decide who would represent the bloc. He said there was a strong view among European leaders that it was for Europe – in the wider sense – “to decide its own arrangements” on security.

articles.title: If Gen Z are asked to go to war, it might not be in the way they expect
articles.summary: Brief letters: Fighting for your country | Starbucks | Sparta | Itching powder
body: Jason Okundaye addresses the issue of whether Britain’s youth would be willing to lay down their lives in defence of our country (Gen Z doesn‘t relish going to war – so what! You should worry more about the reckless generations that do, 10 November). A more likely scenario is that they will be asked to fight and die for the sake of a Nato ally on Russia’s border, such as Poland or Lithuania.Matthew J SmithNew Malden, London
